title: Pakistan Just Bombed Afghanistan for the Second Time This Month. India Told Islamabad to Stop Blaming Everyone Else.
excerpt: After a Karachi Rangers attack killed three soldiers, Pakistan struck militant hideouts across three Afghan provinces. Kabul says the bombs hit civilians. India called Pakistan’s attempt to link it to the Karachi assault ‘baseless.’
body:
A suicide bomber and gunmen stormed the Sindh Rangers’ Bhittai Wing headquarters in Karachi’s Gulistan-e-Jauhar neighbourhood on Saturday night. The attackers detonated an explosive at the entrance, then opened fire. Three Rangers personnel were killed and four wounded before security forces — reinforced by Special Security Unit commandos and the Anti-Terrorist Force — ended the assault in roughly 90 minutes.

Three militants died in the gunfight. A fourth, whom the Pakistani military identified as an Afghan national, was captured alive and wounded. Jamaat-ul-Ahrar, a splinter faction of the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack, which marked Karachi’s most significant security incident since an explosion targeting a Chinese convoy in October 2024.

## Pakistan’s Retaliatory Strikes

Within 24 hours of the Karachi attack, Islamabad launched what it termed “calibrated strikes.” Information Minister Attaullah Tarar announced on X that Pakistani jets hit targets in three Afghan provinces — Paktia, Paktika, and Kunar — destroying what he described as “terrorist camps and safe havens” and killing 25 militants. A separate ground operation in the Bajaur district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa killed four more fighters linked to Jamaat-ul-Ahrar, bringing the total reported militant casualties to 29.

This marked Pakistan’s second set of airstrikes on Afghan territory this month, following similar actions earlier in May, indicating a growing pattern of cross-border military responses. These escalating military actions have raised concerns among the Indian diaspora, particularly those with family in the region, about the potential for broader instability.

## Kabul’s Version Is Very Different



> **"Residents in the Samkani district described a "double-tap" scenario, where, after locals rushed to help the wounded from the initial strike, Pakistani jets bombed the same location again."**


Afghanistan’s Taliban government painted a starkly different picture of the strikes. Government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat stated that the strikes killed 38 civilians and injured 163, including women and children. According to Afghan officials, most of the casualties resulted from a single strike on a home in Paktia province that killed 28 people and wounded 158.

Residents in the Samkani district described a "double-tap" scenario, where, after locals rushed to help the wounded from the initial strike, Pakistani jets bombed the same location again. Deputy district head Khalid Ahmad Sajad confirmed this sequence at a press conference.


![Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/River_Swat%2C_KPK.jpg/3840px-River_Swat%2C_KPK.jpg)


Deputy Information Minister Mohajer Farahi went further, warning that the “attack will certainly be avenged at the appropriate time.” This strong language raises the spectre of a broader escalation between two nuclear neighbours already engaged in a slow-burning conflict. Pakistan and Afghanistan fought their worst battle in years in February, and internationally mediated talks — including Chinese-hosted discussions in April — have failed to produce a lasting ceasefire.

## India Tells Pakistan to ‘Look Inwards’

Before the retaliatory strikes, some Pakistani officials — including Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi — had attempted to link India to the Karachi assault. India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) dismissed these allegations outright.

“We have seen Pakistani reports making baseless allegations against India regarding the recent incident in Karachi. We categorically reject them,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. “Instead of pointing fingers at others, Pakistan would do better to look inwards, take credible action against the terror infrastructure on its territory and rid itself of its proclivity to rely on terrorism as an instrument of state policy.”

The MEA’s response was swift, unambiguous, and notably more assertive than India’s usual diplomatic language on Pakistan — a reflection of New Delhi’s hardened stance since Operation Sindoor earlier this year. This firm diplomatic posture is closely watched by the Indian diaspora, particularly those with business interests or family ties in the region, as it signals India's commitment to regional stability and its approach to cross-border terrorism.

## What This Means for the Region

Pakistan is trapped in a worsening cycle of violence. The TTP — distinct from the Afghan Taliban but allied with it — has intensified attacks on security forces, particularly in the border provinces. Islamabad blames Kabul for harbouring the militants who plan these assaults. The Afghan Taliban denies the charge, calling militancy Pakistan’s internal problem.

Each cross-border strike risks pulling the two former allies into a wider confrontation, with the Afghan Taliban now explicitly threatening retaliation. Analysts warn that the latest escalation could torpedo what little remains of diplomatic engagement between the two countries.

For India, the immediate concern is stability in a region where roughly 9 million Indian workers are employed across the Gulf states, and where the fallout from a Pakistan-Afghanistan war could scramble migration routes, energy markets, and counterterrorism cooperation. The longer-term concern is more straightforward: a nuclear-armed neighbour that responds to every security failure by pointing its finger across the border. For NRIs, particularly those engaged in trade or remittances to India, regional instability can have direct economic implications, affecting everything from travel plans to the security of investments and the well-being of family members back home. The potential for increased border tensions also raises questions for dual citizens and those with family in the subcontinent regarding travel advisories and the overall security landscape.
